nameStory: The "rotund-collared" part of this beetle's name comes from its distinctively rounded, bulging pronotum - that's the shield-like section right behind its head that looks like a puffy collar. Soldier beetles earned their military nickname because many species wear bright colors that reminded early naturalists of military dress uniforms, though this particular species tends toward more subdued tones.
description: The Rotund-collared Soldier Beetle is a medium-sized beetle that belongs to a large family of beneficial predatory insects. Like other soldier beetles, it has a somewhat soft, flexible body compared to many beetles, with wing covers that don't completely hide its abdomen. These beetles are active hunters that patrol flowers and foliage looking for small insects to eat. Adults typically measure around half an inch in length and have the characteristic rounded pronotum that gives them their name.

idTips.label: Rounded pronotum
idTips.description: The shield-like section behind the head is noticeably bulging and rounded, feeling smooth to the touch and creating a distinctive puffy collar appearance

idTips.label: Soft wing covers
idTips.description: Unlike hard-shelled beetles, the wing covers feel somewhat leathery and flexible when gently touched, and don't extend all the way to cover the entire abdomen

idTips.label: Subdued coloration
idTips.description: Typically displays muted browns, oranges, or yellows rather than the bright reds and oranges of some flashier soldier beetles

idTips.label: Active hunting behavior
idTips.description: Moves deliberately across flowers and leaves with purpose, often pausing to grab small prey with visible chewing motions

idTips.label: Antennae length
idTips.description: Thread-like antennae extend roughly half the length of the body and are constantly moving to sense the environment

habitat: Look for Rotund-collared Soldier Beetles in mixed forests, woodland edges, and meadows throughout New England's lower elevations. They're particularly fond of areas where wildflowers bloom near wooded borders, as these spots provide both hunting grounds for small insects and nectar sources. You'll often spot them on goldenrod, asters, and other composite flowers in late summer.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring but are not yet at peak activity. Look for them on early blooming shrubs and trees where they hunt for aphids and other soft-bodied insects.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly seen. They're actively hunting on flowers and foliage during warm, sunny days, often remaining motionless when temperatures drop or during overcast weather.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, particularly on late-season flowers like goldenrod and asters. They become sluggish as temperatures drop and eventually seek overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off and the species overwinters in earlier life stages. No beetle activity to observe during the cold months.

funFact: Despite being called soldier beetles, these insects are actually peacekeepers in the garden world - they're voracious predators that can consume dozens of aphids, caterpillars, and other pest insects in a single day, making them worth their weight in gold to farmers and gardeners.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other soldier beetles in the Cantharidae family, but the distinctly rounded, bulging pronotum sets this species apart from its flatter-collared relatives. Memory trick: "Rotund collar, round beetle" - if the pronotum looks like it's been inflated, you've likely found your rotund-collared friend.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Pacificanthia might suggest a Pacific coast connection, but this beetle is actually well-established in eastern North America including New England. This naming quirk sometimes confuses naturalists who expect geographic names to match current distributions.
compareHints: As the only Pacificanthia species in New England, this beetle stands out from other local soldier beetles primarily by its inflated pronotum. While species like the Common Red Soldier Beetle have flatter, more angular pronota, the Rotund-collared maintains its distinctive puffy collar appearance. It also tends toward more muted colors than many of its flashier soldier beetle cousins.
